one_liner: Default-settings OpenJDK 25 running benchLANG's binary trees about 2.9x faster than per-node malloc/free C and 3.3x faster than new/delete C++.
what_it_does: A row from benchLANG, a small 19-language benchmark, not a library. The binary-trees workload builds a depth-19 stretch tree, a depth-18 long-lived tree and then 2^(22-d) short-lived trees at each even depth d from 4 to 18 (68,332,206 nodes in all, counted from the loop bounds in the source), sums each with a recursive check and discards it. The Java version is a static final class Node with final left, right and long item fields in one bench.java, compiled with javac and run as plain 'java bench' with no flags. Using the result means writing the allocation-heavy part in Java; nothing here links into a C++ program.
how_it_is_fast: Memory management, not code generation. Likely mechanism (inference, consistent with the README's 'GC runtimes collect when they like'): HotSpot hands out each Node by bumping a pointer in a thread-local allocation buffer, and the default G1 collector's young collections copy only live objects, so the millions of dead short-lived trees cost nothing to reclaim; only the long-lived tree survives. The C and C++ programs call glibc malloc or operator new per node and then walk every tree a second time (free_tree) to free or delete each node inside the timer. Per node that is about 5.1 ns for Java against 14.8 ns for C and 16.8 ns for C++ (derived from page data over 68.3M nodes).
when_to_use: You already run on the JVM and are tempted to move a builder of many small, short-lived objects (parse trees, temporary graphs, ASTs) to native code: with default settings HotSpot beat naive malloc/free C by about 2.9x here.
Throughput or batch jobs that allocate and drop whole object graphs at once, where wall time matters more than memory footprint or pause times.
Machines with plenty of RAM and idle cores, which the JVM's default heap sizing and parallel GC workers exploit.
As a data point that per-node malloc/free, not the language, is the bottleneck of a C or C++ tree builder.
when_not_to_use: As evidence that Java beats tuned C++: benchLANG has no arena or pool variant. In LangArena's Binarytrees::Arena test a C index arena grown by realloc (C/Gcc/Fast 0.255 s) beats HotSpot's object tree (Binarytrees::Obj, 0.479 s), though a C++ std::vector arena without reserve does not (best 0.512 s); std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource or a bump allocator would also remove the per-node frees and the second traversal here (inference, not measured in benchLANG).
Memory-constrained deployments: whole-process peak RSS was 987.8 MiB for Java against 33.3 MiB for C and 35.4 MiB for C++, about 30x, and the JVM is not counted in any binary size.
Latency-sensitive code with tight pause or footprint budgets: the table reports no pause times and no per-workload CPU time.
Recursion- or string-heavy code: the same Java program loses Fibonacci(45) (4.109 s vs 1.694 s for C) and strings (4.075 s vs 2.132 s) and the suite overall (13.536 s vs 9.762 s).

integration.dependencies: A JDK: OpenJDK 25.0.4 from nixpkgs-unstable (jdk25 in flake.nix, pinned by the committed flake.lock); no libraries
integration.min_toolchain: OpenJDK 25.0.4 as measured; bench.java itself uses only long-standing language features (final fields, numeric-literal underscores, String.split), so older JDKs should compile it, but only 25.0.4 was measured
integration.platforms: Measured on x86-64 Linux only (flake.nix sets system = x86_64-linux), Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz
integration.thread_safety: Not applicable: single-threaded workload; the JVM runs GC and JIT compiler threads beside it

gotchas: Harness asymmetry behind the margin: C and C++ free every node in a second traversal inside the timer, while Java drops the root and stops its timer with the long-lived tree and the last young-generation garbage still uncollected (the JVM exits right after). The README states this design, so it is a fair description of what is measured, but it compares allocation strategies, not languages.

Extra cores are invisible: CPUx = (user+sys)/wall is computed by analyze_results.sh over the whole process but is left out of the README table, and the raw benchmark_results_*.txt file is never committed (.gitignore ignores '*' and does not re-include .txt), so how much GC and JIT helper-thread CPU the Java run used cannot be checked. Java at 0.347 s is also 2.3x ahead of every other managed or native row (Nim 0.809 s, Bun 0.816 s), an outlier that one run cannot confirm. On a similar test in LangArena (Binarytrees::Obj), HotSpot (OpenJDK 27) restricted to single-threaded SerialGC and a 512 MB heap ran in 0.886 s against 0.479 s with default G1, so GC worker threads and heap size can account for about half of such a margin.

Default JVM ergonomics on a 48 GB machine: no -Xmx or GC flag is passed, so heap and young-generation sizes follow the host's RAM and core count; peak RSS of 987.8 MiB suggests a large young generation and few collections. A smaller container or a fixed heap could change the result (inference, not measured).

One run per language on 3 September 2026, wall time from System.nanoTime() inside the program; binary trees runs last in the same JVM after the other four workloads, so JVM startup is excluded but makeTree and checkTree still JIT-compile inside the timed region. run_benchmarks.sh supports --runs N, but the published table does not use it.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Java's 0.347 s is the largest managed-runtime margin among the catalogued benchLANG binary-trees rows (C# 0.931 s, Bun 0.816 s, OCaml 0.865 s), so it is the strongest of those data points if you are on the JVM; LangArena's Java Binarytrees::Obj entry (0.479 s vs C++ 2.098 s, with -O3 and PGO baselines) is better evidence because it also measures an arena variant that shows where the win ends.
verified_claims_summary: benchLANG's 3 September 2026 run on a Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz (Arch Linux, 48 GB DDR4-3600) timed binary trees at 0.347 s for OpenJDK 25.0.4 with default heap and GC against 1.010 s for C and 1.147 s for C++, both built by GCC 16.2.0 with -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops and allocating each node with malloc/free or new/delete; about 2.9x and 3.3x faster (derived from page data), one run each, with the analyzer checking that all languages print the same checksum.
status_note: Small single-author MIT repo (8 stars, 42 commits, no issues, last commit 2026-09-03) with Nix-pinned toolchains and a committed flake.lock, so anyone can rerun it, but this is one run of one micro-workload whose raw results file and CPU-time column are unpublished.
